overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing One Chapter, Opening the Next
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 13a–13b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the discussion of the priestly watches with the prophets' ruling that Jedaiah's watch keeps precedence even if Yehoyariv's line later returns, and offers Rav Ashi's own resolution to the Second Temple dating puzzle: the six years before Ezra resanctified the land for the Sabbatical cycle simply don't count. A new mishna then sets more Temple minimums and maximums — six inspected lambs kept on hand, examined four days before slaughter per ben Bag Bag, a floor of two trumpets and nine harps with generous ceilings, and exactly one cymbal, never more. Another mishna fixes twelve Levites as the minimum on the singers' platform, with a dispute over whether minor Levites, who join only during the actual singing to sweeten the sound, count toward that number. The daf then closes the tractate's opening chapters entirely and opens a new one: a mishna listing four areas of halakha with both lenient and stringent rulings, starting with the observation that the Torah's flat fifty-sela valuation applies identically to the most beautiful and the most unsightly person, in sharp contrast to a vow of one's actual market price.

slides.title: ⛓️ Finishing the Priestly-Watch Puzzle
slides.subtitle: Two more resolutions to yesterday's dating question

steps.content: 1️⃣ The prophets decreed: even if Yehoyariv's original watch later returned to Eretz Yisrael, Jedaiah's watch — already reconstituted — keeps its precedence as first; Yehoyariv would be subordinate
2️⃣ So the baraita's claim that both Temples fell 'the same way' refers only to shared details (the 9th of Av, a Sunday) — not to which watch was actually on duty
3️⃣ Rav Ashi's separate answer: the six years between the start of the Second Temple's construction and Ezra's arrival, when he resanctified the land, don't count toward the Sabbatical cycle at all
4️⃣ Excluding those six years, the remaining count of years lands the destruction squarely in the year after Shmita — matching the baraita after all

slides.title: 🎵 Do Minor Singers Count Toward the Twelve Levites?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's dissent

lines.speaker: Tanna Kamma
lines.text: No fewer than twelve Levites stand on the platform. Minors may join in SINGING (not instruments) only while the adults sing, adding sweetness with their pure, high voices.

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer b. Ya'akov
lines.text: Minors are NOT counted among the twelve, and they don't even stand on the platform — they stand on the ground, their heads reaching only to between the Levites' feet.

lines.speaker: Naming (Tanna Kamma)
lines.text: Our mishna calls them tza'arei — 'those who cause distress' — since their pure high voices made the grown Levites sound inferior by comparison.

lines.speaker: A baraita disagrees
lines.text: It instead calls them so'adei — 'those who assist' — a gentler name for the same young singers.

slides.title: ⚖️ New Chapter: Leniency and Stringency in a Valuation Vow
slides.subtitle: The same person, two different ways of being valuated

boxes.title: Fixed Torah Valuation (erech)
items: Vowing the fixed valuation of the most beautiful Israelite, OR of the most unsightly
BOTH pay exactly 50 sela — the Torah's flat sum ignores actual appearance or worth

boxes.title: Market Assessment (damim)
items: Vowing instead 'his price is upon me,' as if he were sold as a slave
Payment tracks his ACTUAL market worth — more for the beautiful, less for the unsightly

callout.label: Leniency and stringency:
callout.text: The flat 50-sela erech is lenient for someone actually worth more on the market, and stringent for someone actually worth less — exactly the reverse of the damim-based vow, which is always precise to the person's real value.

summary.principle: As the tractate's early chapters close, its final rulings on the Temple's music — exact minimums and maximums for lambs, trumpets, harps, the single cymbal, and the platform's Levites — give way to a new chapter's opening insight: a Torah-fixed valuation is blind to a person's actual worth, while a market assessment is precisely sensitive to it.

flowSteps.content: ⛓️ Jedaiah's watch keeps precedence regardless; Rav Ashi excludes six pre-Ezra years from the Sabbatical count

columns.content: 🎵 Minor singers: counted toward the 12 and on the platform, or not — a real dispute with two names for the same children
⚖️ New chapter: fixed erech (50 sela flat) vs. damim (actual market worth) — leniency and stringency in the same vow

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: precise floors and ceilings govern the Temple's music, just as a precise contrast between a flat sum and a variable market value governs how a person is valuated

quiz.q: What did the prophets decree about the precedence of the priestly watch of Jedaiah?
o: That Jedaiah's watch would be dissolved once Yehoyariv's line returned
That even if Yehoyariv's original watch later returned to Eretz Yisrael, Jedaiah would retain its place as first, and Yehoyariv would be subordinate to it
That the two watches would alternate service annually
That only Yehoyariv's watch could ever serve as first
quiz.e: The prophets protected the newly reconstituted watch of Jedaiah's precedence permanently, even against the possibility that the original leading watch of Yehoyariv might later return.

quiz.q: According to Rav Ashi's resolution, why does the 420-year span of the Second Temple still work out to a destruction in the year after Shmita?
o: Because the Second Temple actually stood for a different number of years
The six years between the start of construction and Ezra's arrival, when he resanctified the land, are not counted toward the Sabbatical cycle at all
Because Rabbi Yehuda's Jubilee-counting method is applied throughout
Because the calculation ignores leap years entirely
quiz.e: Rav Ashi excludes the six years before Ezra resanctified the land (since the Sabbatical cycle was not in effect during that period), which shifts the final total to land in the year after Shmita.

quiz.q: According to ben Bag Bag, from where is it derived that the daily offering requires inspection four days before its slaughter?
o: A direct verse stating the exact number of days
A shared use of the word 'safeguard' (מִשְׁמֶרֶת/תִּשְׁמְרוּ) links the daily offering's verse to the Paschal offering's, which explicitly requires four days of inspection
An oral tradition with no textual basis
A comparison to the inspection required for a blemished animal
quiz.e: Ben Bag Bag derives the four-day requirement through a verbal analogy based on the shared root of 'safeguard' in the verses about the daily offering and the Paschal offering.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is unique about the cymbal in the Temple orchestra compared to the trumpets or harps?
o: There is exactly one, and none may ever be added — unlike the flexible minimums and unlimited maximums for trumpets and harps
The cymbal has no fixed number at all
The cymbal could be played by anyone, unlike other instruments
The cymbal was banned from Temple use entirely
quiz.e: Unlike trumpets (2 to 120) and harps (9 and unlimited), the mishna fixes the cymbal at exactly one — played by a single person striking the paired cymbals together.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna's example of leniency and stringency in arakhin, what is true of someone who vows the fixed valuation (erech) of both the most beautiful and the most unsightly Israelite?
o: The payment varies significantly based on actual appearance
Both cases require exactly the same fixed sum of fifty sela, regardless of actual appearance or market worth
Only the valuation of the beautiful person is valid
Neither valuation is ever collected
quiz.e: The mishna's example shows that the Torah's flat fixed valuation of fifty sela applies identically to both the most attractive and the least attractive person, unlike a vow based on actual market price (damim).
